stem: A pipeline step spins up a coding agent to fix a failing lint rule across a repo. The team's loop-control code inspects the assistant's reply for the substring "done" to decide whether to stop sending requests. Twice this month the pipeline hung for 20 minutes because the model's final message happened to read "the lint config is now fine" without the literal word "done" anywhere in it, so the loop kept invoking tools well past the point the fix was actually complete. What is the most direct fix?
explanation: The loop should branch on the structured `stop_reason` field (`tool_use` vs. `end_turn`), not on substring-matching free-form reply text — that's the exact brittleness the exam flags, and it's what caused this pipeline hang.

choices.text: Branch on response.stop_reason instead of substring-matching the reply text
choices.reasoning: Correct: this swaps the brittle text-matching heuristic for the structured, purpose-built signal that reliably indicates whether Claude wants to act further — stopping specifically when stop_reason is anything other than tool_use.

choices.text: Expand the substring list to also match "fine", "complete", "finished", and other synonyms
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this only patches the specific miss without fixing the underlying fragility — any future phrasing the list doesn't anticipate reproduces the same hang.

choices.text: Lower the model's temperature so it always phrases completion the same way
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: temperature doesn't guarantee a fixed completion phrase, and the loop still shouldn't depend on wording at all.

choices.text: Add a fixed 5-iteration cap so the pipeline can never hang longer than a bounded number of turns
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a fixed cap risks cutting off legitimate longer fixes and doesn't address the actual defect — the loop is watching the wrong signal entirely.

choices.text: Have a second Claude call classify whether the first call's reply means "finished"
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this adds cost and a new source of unreliability to work around a problem that a structured field already solves directly.

choices.text: Increase max_tokens so the model has more room to state completion clearly
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: output length isn't why the substring match failed; the reply simply used different wording, which no length increase fixes.

stem: An architect is designing a system that always performs the same three steps for every incoming brief: pull the latest filings for a named company, extract key financial figures, then format them into a one-page summary. No branching, no adaptive follow-up — every brief goes through exactly these three steps in this order. A colleague proposes a full coordinator-plus-dynamic-decomposition architecture "to be safe." What should the architect push back with?
explanation: A fixed, always-the-same-order sequence is the textbook prompt-chaining case; reaching for dynamic decomposition or a coordinator when the work is mechanical and fully known in advance is the documented over-engineering trap — the simplest pattern that fits should win.

choices.text: Prompt chaining fits — this is a fixed three-step sequence with no adaptive branching
choices.reasoning: Correct: the work described has no findings-dependent branching at all — it's the exact shape prompt chaining is built for, and adding a coordinator/dynamic-decomposition layer only adds cost and complexity without benefit.

choices.text: Dynamic decomposition is always safer regardless of task shape, so the colleague is right
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this ignores that the task has no genuine open-endedness — reaching for the more sophisticated pattern here is exactly the flagged anti-pattern, not a safety improvement.

choices.text: The system should use routing instead, since there are three distinct steps to choose between
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: all three steps run for every brief in the same order — nothing is being classified or chosen between, which rules out routing.

choices.text: The system should use parallel subagents, since financial extraction and summary formatting are independent
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: formatting the summary depends on the extracted figures being available first — these steps aren't independent, which rules out parallel subagents.

choices.text: The coordinator's added complexity is worth it purely because financial data is high-stakes
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: stakes alone don't determine which orchestration pattern fits; the deciding factor is the actual shape of the work, which here is a fixed, non-adaptive sequence.

choices.text: Neither pattern applies; the task should be handled with a single unstructured prompt with no orchestration at all
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this discards the reliability benefit of separating fixed steps, which prompt chaining specifically provides over one large unstructured prompt.

stem: Incoming tickets must be sorted into billing, technical, and account-access buckets, each handled by a differently-configured agent. For the first year this worked well. Recently, a wave of tickets about a new "data export" feature don't cleanly fit any of the three buckets, and support leads report the system keeps forcing them into "technical" even when agents mis-resolve them. What does this recurring mis-resolution most likely indicate about the architecture?
explanation: Routing depends on categories staying distinct and stable. A new class of ticket that doesn't fit the existing buckets is exactly the condition under which routing's core assumption breaks down — the category set needs revisiting (e.g. a new bucket, or an escape-hatch category), not a stronger prompt telling the router to try harder.

choices.text: A new, genuinely distinct category has emerged that the routing taxonomy doesn't yet cover
choices.reasoning: Correct: routing's reliability depends on categories staying distinct and stable; an emerging category that doesn't fit existing buckets is precisely the signal that the taxonomy itself needs to change.

choices.text: The routing agent's system prompt needs stronger wording insisting it classify more carefully
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: no amount of prompt wording fixes a category that genuinely doesn't fit any existing bucket — the taxonomy itself is the problem, not classifier effort.

choices.text: The system should switch entirely to parallel subagents that each attempt to resolve every ticket independently
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: parallel subagents address independent workstreams, not a category-taxonomy mismatch — this doesn't fix misclassification at all.

choices.text: The tickets should simply be forced into whichever of the three existing buckets scores highest, regardless of fit
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is exactly what's already happening and causing mis-resolution — forcing an ill-fitting category into an existing bucket doesn't solve the underlying gap.

choices.text: The support team should stop using any orchestration pattern and route every ticket manually going forward
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this abandons automation to work around a fixable taxonomy gap, rather than adjusting the category design.

choices.text: The issue is unrelated to orchestration pattern choice and is purely a model-tier problem
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the symptom described — a new category not fitting — is a category-design issue, not resolved by changing which model tier does the classifying.

stem: A coordinator needs to gather background on three unrelated competitor companies for an independent market-scan report; nothing learned about Company A affects how Company B or C are researched. An engineer implements this by having the coordinator issue one Task call, wait for it to fully return, then issue the next Task call, and so on. Stakeholders complain the report now takes three times as long as expected. What's the fix?
explanation: Because the three research workstreams are genuinely independent, issuing all three Task calls within a single coordinator turn lets them run in parallel, collapsing elapsed time to the slowest single one rather than the sum of all three sequential runs.

choices.text: Issue all three Task calls in one coordinator turn so they run in parallel
choices.reasoning: Correct: for independent workstreams, launching them together makes elapsed time the duration of the slowest one rather than the sum of all three, which is exactly the reported symptom of sequential launch.

choices.text: Switch all three research subtasks to the Batch API to cut costs
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: Batch has no SLA and unpredictable turnaround up to 24 hours — the complaint here is about latency for a report stakeholders are waiting on, which batch would make worse, not better.

choices.text: Merge the three companies into a single subagent prompt covering all of them at once
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this discards the benefit of clean, independent subagent scoping and risks the single subagent conflating findings across the three companies.

choices.text: Give the coordinator a higher-tier model so each sequential Task call completes faster
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a faster model per call reduces but doesn't eliminate the fundamental sequential-sum problem; running the independent calls in parallel addresses the actual architectural cause.

choices.text: Add a fourth subagent to double-check the first three sequentially
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: adding another sequential step increases total elapsed time further, worsening the exact problem being reported.

choices.text: Reduce each subagent's toolset to a single tool to speed up tool selection
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: while narrow toolsets are good practice for role clarity, the reported slowdown is architectural (sequential vs. parallel launch), not a tool-selection latency issue.

stem: A coordinator learns mid-conversation that a customer's account was flagged for a prior fraud investigation. It then spawns a billing-adjustment subagent, prompted only with `{"goal": "process the requested $40 credit"}`, expecting the subagent to "already know" about the fraud flag since it's part of the same overall case. The subagent approves the credit without any special handling. What went wrong architecturally?
explanation: A subagent does not inherit the coordinator's conversation history. Any fact the coordinator already knows that the subagent needs — like the fraud flag here — must be explicitly included in that subagent's prompt; assuming context automatically flows down is a documented, common wrong answer.

choices.text: The fraud flag was never included in the subagent's prompt
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is exactly the documented gotcha — relevant facts the coordinator knows must be explicitly included in a subagent's prompt, since context doesn't flow down on its own.

choices.text: The subagent's model tier was too low to reason about fraud risk
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model tier isn't the described cause; the subagent was never given the fraud-flag information at all, so no tier would have surfaced it.

choices.text: The coordinator should have used a lower temperature when spawning the subagent
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: sampling temperature doesn't affect what information is or isn't included in a subagent's prompt.

choices.text: This is expected and correct behavior — subagents are supposed to operate independently of any prior findings
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: operating independently of irrelevant information is fine, but a fact directly relevant to the task (a fraud flag on the very account being credited) needed to be explicitly passed in, which it wasn't.

choices.text: The subagent needed the Task tool added to escalate on its own initiative
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: adding a tool for the subagent to spawn further subagents doesn't address the root cause — the missing fraud-flag context in its prompt.

choices.text: The billing tool itself is broken and needs a bug fix unrelated to prompt content
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the tool executed the request correctly given what it was told; the failure is upstream, in what context the subagent was given.

stem: One of three parallel research subagents hits a rate-limited external API and returns `[]` — an empty array, indistinguishable in shape from a subagent that searched successfully and genuinely found nothing. The coordinator treats both cases identically and reports the topic as "no relevant findings" in the final synthesis. Weeks later it turns out the rate-limited subagent never actually completed its search. What should the architecture have done differently?
explanation: Empty and failed are not the same outcome and must not be conflated. Subagents should return structured failure context — what was attempted, why it failed, whether retry is worthwhile — so the coordinator can distinguish a genuine empty result from a silent failure and recover appropriately, rather than reporting a false "no findings" conclusion.

choices.text: The subagent should have returned structured failure context instead of an empty array
choices.reasoning: Correct: collapsing a genuine failure into the same shape as a valid empty result is exactly the trap this domain warns about — the fix is a distinct, structured failure shape so the coordinator never mistakes one for the other.

choices.text: The coordinator should have simply retried the rate-limited call an unlimited number of times until it succeeded
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this doesn't address the design flaw that made the failure indistinguishable from success in the first place, and unbounded retries against a rate limit risk making things worse.

choices.text: All three subagents should have shared one combined context window to avoid any of them missing data
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: sharing context doesn't address the actual defect — the output shape not distinguishing failure from a valid empty result.

choices.text: The subagent should have been given a higher-tier model so it wouldn't get rate-limited
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model tier has no bearing on whether an external API rate-limits a request; the fix belongs in the failure-reporting design, not model selection.

choices.text: Nothing — an empty array is always the correct way to report both a valid empty result and a failure
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is precisely the anti-pattern that caused the false conclusion in this scenario — an undifferentiated empty result prevented the coordinator from recovering correctly.

choices.text: The coordinator should have lowered its own confidence score in the final report instead of investigating the empty result
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: adjusting a confidence score doesn't recover the missing search or alert anyone that the subtask actually failed rather than legitimately finding nothing.

stem: A "research" subagent tasked only with locating where a bug originates is given the full 18-tool toolset, including Edit and Write, "in case it needs them." During review, the team finds the subagent has started making speculative code edits mid-investigation, well before its findings were reported back to the coordinator. What is the most likely architectural cause, and the fix?
explanation: Giving a subagent the full toolset instead of the roughly 4-5 tools its role actually needs increases tool-selection complexity and causes role drift — precisely the described failure mode (a research agent editing files because Edit happens to be available). The fix is scoping the subagent's tools narrowly to its actual role.

choices.text: The broad toolset caused role drift; scope the subagent to a narrow read/search-only toolset
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented cause and fix directly — a research-only role should be scoped narrowly, and removing tools irrelevant to its purpose (like Edit) removes the temptation/ability to drift into unrelated actions.

choices.text: The subagent's system prompt needs a stronger instruction telling it not to edit files
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a prompt-level instruction is guidance the model may not perfectly follow; the more reliable fix is removing the capability entirely from the toolset.

choices.text: This is normal behavior and no change is needed — subagents should have access to every tool to avoid being blocked
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is the explicitly documented anti-pattern ("give every agent every tool, just in case"), and the scenario shows exactly the role-drift consequence it causes.

choices.text: The subagent should be given an even broader toolset so it can also run tests to confirm its edits
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: expanding the toolset further compounds the role-drift problem rather than fixing it — a research-only role shouldn't be editing or testing at all.

choices.text: Switch the subagent to a lower-tier model so it's less capable of making edits
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: lowering model capability doesn't remove the Edit/Write tools from its available toolset; the fix is scoping the toolset itself, not degrading the model.

choices.text: Increase the coordinator's max_tokens so it can more thoroughly review the subagent's actions afterward
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: after-the-fact review capacity doesn't prevent the drift from happening; the fix is removing the unnecessary tools up front.

stem: A refund-processing agent's system prompt states: "Always verify the customer's identity before issuing a refund." An incident review finds a refund was issued without identity verification because the model, deep in a long troubleshooting conversation, simply didn't re-apply that instruction on this particular turn. What architectural change would have prevented this specific incident?
explanation: A prerequisite gate makes the precondition structurally unavoidable — the refund tool itself is blocked from being callable until an identity_verified flag is set by an earlier step — rather than depending on the model consistently remembering and applying a system-prompt instruction, which is exactly what failed here.

choices.text: Make identity verification a prerequisite gate the refund tool structurally can't bypass
choices.reasoning: Correct: this converts the instruction into a structural precondition the agent literally cannot bypass, which addresses the exact failure mode described — an instruction not being re-applied reliably.

choices.text: Rewrite the system prompt to repeat the identity-verification instruction in bold at the top and bottom of the prompt
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is still guidance the model may fail to apply consistently, especially deep in a long conversation, which is exactly the failure mode that already occurred.

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples showing identity verification happening correctly
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: few-shot examples improve behavior probabilistically but don't structurally prevent the refund tool from executing without verification — the same failure could recur.

choices.text: Increase the model tier used for the refund agent so it's less likely to forget
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a higher-tier model still isn't a structural guarantee; the incident was caused by an instruction not being enforced, which model capability alone doesn't fix.

choices.text: Log every refund for weekly audit review, without changing whether the tool can be called
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: after-the-fact logging doesn't prevent an unverified refund from executing in the first place; it only helps detect it later.

choices.text: Move the identity-verification instruction from the system prompt into CLAUDE.md
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: CLAUDE.md is still context the model reads and may or may not perfectly follow, not an enforced boundary — moving the instruction's location doesn't make it structurally binding.

stem: A coordinator connects to a third-party MCP server whose "archive_document" tool is annotated `destructiveHint: false`. Trusting this, the coordinator calls the tool freely without any additional permission check, on the assumption the annotation guarantees the action is safe. Later, the tool turns out to permanently delete the original document as part of "archiving." What was the architectural mistake?
explanation: Tool annotation hints are advisory metadata for UI/display purposes, self-reported by the server — not an enforced boundary. A misbehaving or misconfigured server can set them inaccurately, so they should never substitute for an actual permission or side-effect check in code.

choices.text: Trusting destructiveHint as a guarantee rather than unenforced, self-reported metadata
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is exactly the documented gotcha — annotation hints are advisory only; trusting them as a substitute for a real permission/side-effect check is the mistake.

choices.text: Connecting to a third-party MCP server at all, which should never be allowed regardless of annotations
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: third-party MCP servers can be used safely; the specific failure here is trusting an unverified annotation, not the mere act of connecting to an external server.

choices.text: Not routing the archive_document call through a higher-tier model first
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model tier doesn't verify or enforce a tool's actual side effects; the missing safeguard is an independent permission/behavior check, not a smarter model.

choices.text: Failing to set select_count correctly on the tool definition
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: select_count isn't a tool-definition safety concept; it's unrelated to verifying a tool's actual destructive behavior.

choices.text: Using the real-time API instead of the Batch API for this call
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: batch vs. real-time is a latency/cost tradeoff and has no bearing on whether a tool's annotation can be trusted as a safety guarantee.

choices.text: Giving the coordinator too many tools, causing role drift that led to this call
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the failure described isn't a tool-selection/role-drift issue — the coordinator deliberately called the intended tool and was misled by trusting its annotation.

stem: An agent working a multi-day repository migration crashes on day 2 after a laptop restart. To resume, the team's tooling re-injects the entire day-1 raw transcript (every tool call and result) into the new session before continuing. The new session becomes slow to respond and burns a large fraction of its context budget just processing yesterday's history before doing any new work. What should the resumable state have looked like instead?
explanation: The recommended pattern is a structured export of progress — completed_steps, open_gaps, key decisions — not a raw transcript replay. A resumed run should inject only the relevant state, letting new work start immediately without re-processing an entire prior history's worth of tokens.

choices.text: A structured export of completed steps, open gaps, and key decisions
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is exactly the documented fix — structured, compact state lets a resumed session pick up efficiently, avoiding the token and latency cost of replaying an entire raw history.

choices.text: The exact same raw transcript, but compressed with gzip before re-injection
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: compressing the transcript for storage doesn't reduce the token cost once it's decompressed and re-injected into the model's context — the problem is the shape of what's being resumed with, not the storage format.

choices.text: No persisted state at all — the migration should restart entirely from scratch each time it's interrupted
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this discards legitimate day-1 progress entirely, defeating the purpose of a resumable multi-day workflow.

choices.text: Only the final git diff from day 1, with no record of what remains open or why decisions were made
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a diff alone doesn't capture open_gaps or the reasoning behind decisions, which the resumed agent needs to know what's left to do and why prior choices were made.

choices.text: A screenshot of the terminal at the moment of the crash
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a screenshot isn't structured, machine-usable state that a resumed session could inject into its next prompt.

choices.text: The full transcript, but only from the second half of day 1 to save some tokens
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this still re-injects a large raw, unstructured transcript rather than a compact structured summary, and arbitrarily discarding the first half risks losing relevant early decisions.

stem: A synthesized report states "the regulation takes effect in Q3" with no further detail. When a compliance reviewer asks which source that came from and how recent it is, no one on the team can answer — the subagent that found it didn't record anything beyond the bare claim. What should have been required of every subagent's returned claims to prevent this?
explanation: Subagents should attach provenance to every claim: the claim itself, its source id, date, methodology, a confidence signal, and whether it's contested by another source — this is what lets a coordinator or human reviewer later trust or challenge a synthesized answer, which was impossible here without it.

choices.text: Provenance metadata on every claim — source, date, methodology, and confidence
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is exactly the missing requirement — without it, a claim like this can't be traced back or verified, which is precisely the reviewer's blocked question here.

choices.text: A single overall confidence score for the entire report, not tied to any individual claim
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a report-level score still wouldn't tell the reviewer which source a specific claim came from or how recent it is — provenance needs to be per-claim.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the claim text itself — reviewers are expected to independently re-verify every fact from scratch
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: requiring full independent re-verification of every claim defeats the efficiency purpose of collecting provenance up front, and is what actually happened here (the reviewer being stuck).

choices.text: The subagent's raw internal reasoning trace for the entire research session
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a full raw reasoning trace is noisy and unstructured compared to a compact, per-claim source id/date/methodology record, and doesn't guarantee the specific missing detail is easy to find.

choices.text: A timestamp of when the coordinator received the subagent's final report
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the coordinator's receipt time says nothing about the age or origin of the underlying source the claim came from.

choices.text: Nothing — this level of detail isn't expected for a multi-agent research system
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: provenance is explicitly documented as a requirement for exactly this kind of system to remain trustworthy and auditable.

stem: A support system runs its full multi-agent research pipeline — coordinator plus three parallel research subagents — for every incoming question, including simple ones like "what are your business hours?" which the coordinator could answer directly from a static, well-known fact. Customers report the chat feels sluggish even for trivial questions. What should the architect change?
explanation: Running the full multi-agent pipeline for a simple factual lookup the coordinator could answer directly is a documented anti-pattern — orchestration overhead should be proportional to the complexity of the work, not applied uniformly to every request regardless of how simple it is.

choices.text: Let the coordinator answer simple, well-known facts directly and skip the full pipeline
choices.reasoning: Correct: this directly fixes the reported sluggishness by scaling orchestration overhead to actual task complexity instead of applying the same heavy pipeline to every request.

choices.text: Add a fourth parallel subagent so simple questions get answered faster through more parallelism
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: adding more subagents to an already-unnecessary pipeline for a trivial question increases overhead rather than reducing the reported latency.

choices.text: Switch the entire pipeline to the Batch API to reduce cost
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: Batch has no SLA and isn't suitable for a live, user-facing chat interaction the customer is waiting on synchronously — this would make the sluggishness worse, not better.

choices.text: Keep the pipeline as-is; slowness is an unavoidable cost of using multi-agent research
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the slowness here is a direct, fixable consequence of over-applying the pipeline to simple lookups, not an unavoidable property of multi-agent systems in general.

choices.text: Give each research subagent a broader toolset so it can resolve trivial questions faster
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a broader toolset per subagent doesn't address the core issue — that the full pipeline shouldn't be invoked at all for a simple, directly-answerable fact.

choices.text: Move business-hours questions to a higher-tier model within the same pipeline
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: upgrading model tier within an unnecessarily heavy pipeline still runs the full multi-agent overhead for a question that didn't need any of it.
